questions.stem: Why does show dbs display admin, config, and local on a fresh server but omit a newly selected use testLabDB database?

options.text: Lazy disk materialization — show dbs lists only databases holding physical data written on disk
Projection access masking — show dbs hides user databases unless an explicit filter is supplied
Deferred catalog flush — show dbs updates its list only after db.dropDatabase() is executed

questions.rationale: The show dbs command lists only databases that physically hold data on the server (admin, config, local), whereas use testLabDB only selects the name in memory until a collection write materializes it on disk. (Key Takeaway: show dbs excludes unwritten in-memory database contexts.)

questions.stem: What does the shell variable `db` evaluate to inside an active `mongosh` session?

options.text: Active database pointer — displays the name of the database currently targeted by `use`
Server process status — outputs the uptime and port of the running `mongod` daemon
Collection list — enumerates every collection stored inside the active namespace

questions.rationale: Typing `db` in `mongosh` returns the name of the currently selected database pointer in memory (defaulting to `test` before `use <db>` is called). (Key Takeaway: `db` references the active session database context.)

questions.stem: Why does a newly selected database via `use schoolDB` not appear immediately in `show dbs` output?

options.text: Permission lock — `show dbs` hides user databases until `db.auth()` is executed
Lazy allocation — MongoDB allocates zero disk storage until the first document or collection write occurs
Cache delay — `mongosh` refreshes the catalog only after restarting the shell

questions.rationale: MongoDB uses lazy database instantiation: `use schoolDB` only switches the in-memory session pointer and allocates disk files only when the first collection or document is written. (Key Takeaway: Empty databases with zero bytes on disk are omitted from `show dbs`.)

questions.stem: Which three built-in system databases are pre-populated in a standard MongoDB server deployment?

options.text: `admin`, `config`, and `local` — reserved system databases managing auth, sharding/metadata, and instance state
`root`, `master`, and `tempdb` — legacy relational catalog schemas imported at startup
`system`, `public`, and `default` — user-facing namespaces created for guest connections

questions.rationale: Every MongoDB deployment maintains `admin` (authentication and global roles), `config` (cluster/shard metadata), and `local` (instance-local replication/oplog data) alongside user databases. (Key Takeaway: `admin`, `config`, and `local` are MongoDB's core system databases.)

questions.stem: What is the return value and recoverability when db.students.drop() executes on an existing students collection?

options.text: Reversible soft delete — returns the dropped document count and allows undo via db.undoDrop()
Irreversible removal — returns true and permanently deletes the collection, documents, and indexes
Deferred archive — moves students to the local database and returns an archive cursor object

questions.rationale: Executing db.students.drop() returns true (or false if the collection did not exist) and permanently removes the collection, its documents, and its indexes; this action cannot be undone. (Key Takeaway: Dropping a collection via drop() returns true and is permanent and irreversible.)

questions.stem: When is calling `db.createCollection(name, options)` required instead of relying on implicit creation on first insert?

options.text: Standard CRUD workloads — every collection must be pre-declared before `insertOne()` can run
Capped collections or schema validation — when configuring fixed-size circular buffers (`capped: true`) or `$jsonSchema` rules
Primary key generation — when enabling automatic 12-byte `_id: ObjectId` assignment

questions.rationale: While normal collections are created implicitly on first write, `db.createCollection(name, options)` is required upfront when specifying options such as `capped: true`, `size`, `max`, or validator rules. (Key Takeaway: Use `db.createCollection()` to configure capped collections or validators.)

questions.stem: How does a capped collection (`{ capped: true, size: 1048576, max: 500 }`) handle new inserts once its byte `size` or document `max` limit is reached?

options.text: FIFO circular overwrite — automatically evicts the oldest documents in insertion order to make room for new writes
Write rejection error — throws a `CollectionFullException` until `deleteMany()` frees space
Dynamic shard split — doubles the `size` ceiling automatically on disk

questions.rationale: Capped collections behave as fixed-size circular buffers that preserve insertion order and automatically overwrite the oldest documents (FIFO) without manual deletion. (Key Takeaway: Capped collections evict oldest documents in FIFO order when full.)

questions.stem: What is the return value and effect of executing `db.students.drop()` on an existing `students` collection?

options.text: Returns `true` and permanently removes the `students` collection container, all its documents, and all its indexes
Returns `{ deletedCount: n }` while keeping the empty `students` collection and its `_id` index intact
Drops the entire parent database along with every other collection in the namespace

questions.rationale: `db.<collection>.drop()` completely removes the target collection metadata, all documents, and all associated B-tree indexes, returning `true` on success (or `false` if the collection did not exist). (Key Takeaway: `db.collection.drop()` removes both data and indexes for that collection.)

questions.stem: Which payload structure is valid when inserting a student record with an embedded array of subjects via insertOne()?

options.text: Single BSON document object — passes key-value pairs including subjects: ["Math", "Science"]
Unkeyed flat value array — passes ["Rahul", 9, "Math", "Science"] without any field names
Update operator wrapper — passes { $push: { subjects: "Math" } } directly inside insertOne()

questions.rationale: The insertOne() method accepts a single BSON document object whose fields can hold strings, numbers, and arrays such as subjects: ["Math", "Science"]. (Key Takeaway: insertOne() accepts a rich BSON document with nested arrays.)

questions.stem: What argument structure must be passed to `db.students.insertMany()` to ingest multiple documents in a single network round-trip?

options.text: Array of document objects — `db.students.insertMany([ { name: "A" }, { name: "B" } ])` wrapped in square brackets
Comma-separated objects — `db.students.insertMany({ name: "A" }, { name: "B" })` without array brackets
Nested `$batch` operator — `db.students.insertMany({ $batch: [ ... ] })`

questions.rationale: `insertMany()` requires a JavaScript array `[ doc1, doc2, ... ]` as its first parameter; passing bare comma-separated objects causes the second object to be interpreted as the `options` parameter. (Key Takeaway: Always pass an array `[...]` of documents to `insertMany()`.)

questions.stem: How is the 12-byte `_id: ObjectId` structured when MongoDB automatically generates a primary key for an inserted document?

options.text: 4-byte Unix timestamp + 5-byte random process/machine value + 3-byte incrementing counter (24 hex characters)
6-byte IPv4 address + 6-byte sequential auto-increment integer managed by a central lock table
12-byte SHA-256 hash computed strictly from the document's JSON field names

questions.rationale: Every 12-byte BSON `ObjectId` (rendered as 24 hexadecimal characters) consists of a 4-byte creation timestamp, a 5-byte random value unique to the machine/process, and a 3-byte monotonically incrementing counter. (Key Takeaway: `ObjectId` is a 12-byte identifier: 4B timestamp + 5B random + 3B counter.)

questions.stem: Why are `insertOne()` and `insertMany()` preferred over the legacy `db.collection.insert()` method in modern MongoDB drivers?

options.text: Explicit intent & standardized acknowledgment — they return `{ acknowledged: true, insertedId / insertedIds }` and enforce modern CRUD spec compliance
Bypassing `_id` uniqueness — `insertOne()` allows duplicate `_id` values whereas `insert()` throws an error
Schema enforcement — `insert()` only accepts strings whereas `insertOne()` accepts BSON objects

questions.rationale: `insert()` is deprecated because it ambiguously accepts either a single object or an array and returns legacy `WriteResult` objects, whereas `insertOne()` and `insertMany()` provide clear type safety and return `insertedId`/`insertedIds`. (Key Takeaway: Prefer `insertOne()` and `insertMany()` over deprecated `insert()`.)

questions.stem: What does the query db.students.findOne({ age: { $gte: 18 } }, { name: 1, _id: 0 }) return?

options.text: Multi-document cursor — streams every student aged 18 or older containing only the name field
Full unprojected document — returns the first match with all fields because findOne() ignores projection
Single projected document — returns only the first matching student object containing just the name field

questions.rationale: The findOne(query, projection) method returns a single document (the first match, or null) shaped by the projection { name: 1, _id: 0 } rather than a cursor over every match. (Key Takeaway: findOne() with a projection returns only the first matching projected document.)

questions.stem: What is the fundamental return-type difference between `db.students.find({ age: 18 })` and `db.students.findOne({ age: 18 })`?

options.text: `find()` returns an iterable cursor pointer (supporting `.sort()`, `.skip()`, `.limit()`), whereas `findOne()` returns a single document object (or `null`)
`findOne()` returns a cursor limited to 1 batch, whereas `find()` returns a single merged JSON string
Both return cursors, but `findOne()` automatically strips the `_id` field from the output

questions.rationale: `find()` always returns a cursor (even if 0 or 1 document matches), allowing cursor methods like `.sort()`, `.skip()`, `.limit()`, and `.pretty()`, whereas `findOne()` resolves immediately to the first document object or `null`. (Key Takeaway: `find()` returns a cursor; `findOne()` returns a document or `null`.)

questions.stem: How does MongoDB evaluate a multi-field filter document such as `db.students.find({ age: 18, grade: "A" })`?

options.text: Implicit logical AND — returns only documents where `age` equals `18` AND `grade` equals `"A"` simultaneously
Implicit logical OR — returns documents matching either `age: 18` OR `grade: "A"`
Sequential fallback — searches for `age: 18` first and checks `grade: "A"` only if zero documents match

questions.rationale: Comma-separated key-value pairs inside a query filter object are combined using an implicit logical `AND`, requiring every specified condition to match. (Key Takeaway: Multiple fields in `{ field1: v1, field2: v2 }` form an implicit AND query.)

questions.stem: Why does calling `db.students.findOne({ age: 18 }).pretty()` throw a `TypeError` in the MongoDB shell?

options.text: `.pretty()` is a cursor method and `findOne()` returns a resolved BSON document (or `null`), not a cursor
`.pretty()` requires passing `{ indent: 2 }` when chained after `findOne()`
`findOne()` only supports `.sort()` and `.limit()`, not `.pretty()`

questions.rationale: Because `findOne()` returns a document object directly rather than a cursor, cursor prototype methods such as `.pretty()`, `.sort()`, `.skip()`, and `.limit()` cannot be chained to `findOne()`. (Key Takeaway: `.pretty()` can only be chained on a `find()` cursor.)

questions.stem: How does the filter { $or: [{ age: { $gte: 19 } }, { name: "Rahul" }] } evaluate a document { name: "Rahul", age: 16 }?

options.text: Document matches — $or succeeds whenever at least one sub-condition in its array is satisfied
Document is excluded — $or requires every sub-condition in its array to evaluate to true
Query throws error — $or cannot combine a numeric comparison with a string equality check

questions.rationale: The logical $or operator matches a document whenever at least one condition in its array is satisfied; since name: "Rahul" is true, the document matches regardless of age. (Key Takeaway: $or requires only one sub-condition in its array to evaluate to true.)

questions.stem: Which projection document returns ONLY the `name` field of each student while hiding `_id` and all other fields?

options.text: `{ name: 1, _id: 0 }` — explicitly includes `name` (`1`) and suppresses the default `_id` field (`0`)
`{ name: 1 }` — includes `name` and automatically excludes `_id`
`{ name: 1, age: 0 }` — mixes inclusion of `name` with exclusion of `age`

questions.rationale: In MongoDB projections, `_id` is always returned by default unless explicitly excluded via `_id: 0`. Mixing inclusion (`1`) and exclusion (`0`) on regular fields is invalid, except for `{ <field>: 1, _id: 0 }`. (Key Takeaway: Use `{ field: 1, _id: 0 }` to return only specific fields without `_id`.)

questions.stem: In what canonical order does the MongoDB query engine execute `.limit(5)`, `.skip(10)`, and `.sort({ age: -1 })` when all three are chained on a `find()` cursor?

options.text: `sort()` first -> `skip()` second -> `limit()` third, regardless of the syntactic chaining order in the shell
`limit()` first -> `sort()` second -> `skip()` third, sorting only the first 5 documents
Strictly left-to-right in the exact textual order written by the developer

questions.rationale: The MongoDB query planner normalizes cursor modifiers so that `.sort()` is always applied to the matching set first, `.skip()` advances past the offset second, and `.limit()` caps the returned page size last. (Key Takeaway: Cursor execution order is always `sort` -> `skip` -> `limit`.)

questions.stem: Which query filter retrieves all students whose `age` is strictly greater than `18` using MongoDB's comparison operator syntax?

options.text: `db.students.find({ age: { $gt: 18 } })` — nests the `$gt` operator object inside the `age` field
`db.students.find({ $gt: { age: 18 } })` — places `$gt` at the top level outside the field name
`db.students.find({ age: "> 18" })` — passes a relational comparison string literal

questions.rationale: Field-level comparison operators (`$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte`, `$ne`, `$in`, `$nin`) are nested inside the target field's value object: `{ <field>: { $<operator>: <value> } }`. (Key Takeaway: Comparison operators follow `{ field: { $gt: value } }` syntax.)

questions.module_title: Field Modification & In-Place Update Operators (CRUD Update)
questions.stem: What is the exact effect of running db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $pull: { subjects: "Science" } })?

options.text: Targeted element removal — removes "Science" from subjects while keeping other elements intact
Whole array field deletion — deletes the entire subjects array property from Rahul's document
Whole document deletion — deletes Rahul's entire student document because "Science" matched

questions.rationale: The $pull operator removes matching values ("Science") from an array field (subjects) on the first matched document without deleting other array elements or the document itself. (Key Takeaway: $pull removes specified elements from an array field.)

questions.module_title: Field Modification & In-Place Update Operators (CRUD Update)
questions.stem: Which atomic update operator increments a numeric `age` field by `1` in-place without reading the document into client memory first?

options.text: `{ $inc: { age: 1 } }` — atomically adds the specified positive or negative delta to a numeric field
`{ $set: { age: +1 } }` — overwrites the `age` field with the literal number `1`
`{ $push: { age: 1 } }` — appends `1` to an array field rather than incrementing a number

questions.rationale: `$inc` atomically increments (or decrements when given a negative number) a numeric field on the server, avoiding read-modify-write race conditions; `$set: { age: +1 }` would overwrite `age` with `1`. (Key Takeaway: Use `$inc` for atomic numeric increments and decrements.)

questions.module_title: Field Modification & In-Place Update Operators (CRUD Update)
questions.stem: Which pair of update operators adds an element to an array field vs. removes matching elements from an array field?

options.text: `$push` appends a value to an array, whereas `$pull` removes all array elements matching a specified value or condition
`$set` appends to an array, whereas `$unset` removes a single element while keeping the array
`$add` inserts into an array, whereas `$drop` deletes an element from the array

questions.rationale: In MongoDB updates, `$push` appends an item to an array field (e.g., `{ $push: { subjects: "History" } }`), while `$pull` removes matching items from an array field (e.g., `{ $pull: { subjects: "Math" } }`). `$unset` deletes the entire field key from the document. (Key Takeaway: `$push` appends to arrays; `$pull` removes matching elements from arrays.)

questions.module_title: Field Modification & In-Place Update Operators (CRUD Update)
questions.stem: What happens when `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Kiran" }, { $set: { age: 20 } }, { upsert: true })` runs and no document with `name: "Kiran"` exists?

options.text: Inserts a new document `{ name: "Kiran", age: 20 }` with a newly generated `_id` and returns `upsertedId`
Returns `{ matchedCount: 0, modifiedCount: 0 }` without modifying the collection
Throws a `DocumentNotFound` exception because `updateOne` requires an existing match

questions.rationale: Setting `{ upsert: true }` creates and inserts a new document combining the equality filter fields and the `$set` update modifiers when zero documents match the query filter. (Key Takeaway: `upsert: true` inserts a new document when no match is found.)

questions.stem: If a developer wants to remove all students in grade: 7 while leaving students in grades 8, 9, and 10 untouched, which command is required?

options.text: db.students.deleteOne({ grade: 7 }) — removes only the first matching student in grade 7
db.students.deleteMany({ grade: 7 }) — removes every student document where grade equals 7
db.students.deleteMany({}) — removes all student documents across every grade in students

questions.rationale: Calling db.students.deleteMany({ grade: 7 }) deletes every document that matches the filter { grade: 7 } while preserving documents with other grades. (Key Takeaway: Filtered deleteMany(filter) removes all documents matching the specified criteria.)

questions.stem: What is the critical structural difference between running `db.students.deleteMany({})` and `db.students.drop()`?

options.text: `deleteMany({})` removes all documents but keeps the collection container and B-tree indexes intact, whereas `drop()` destroys the collection and all its indexes
`deleteMany({})` drops all indexes while keeping documents, whereas `drop()` removes only the first document
Both commands are identical in execution speed, index retention, and return value

questions.rationale: `deleteMany({})` scans and deletes every document while preserving the collection namespace and its B-tree indexes in memory/disk; `db.students.drop()` instantly frees the entire collection container and destroys all indexes. (Key Takeaway: `deleteMany({})` preserves indexes; `drop()` destroys the collection and its indexes.)

questions.stem: If 5 documents in `students` have `{ age: 19 }`, how many documents are removed by `db.students.deleteOne({ age: 19 })`?

options.text: Strictly 1 document — removes only the first document that matches `{ age: 19 }` and stops
All 5 documents — removes every document matching `{ age: 19 }`
0 documents — throws an `AmbiguousMatchError` when more than one document matches the filter

questions.rationale: `deleteOne(filter)` deletes at most a single document—the first one matching the filter in scan order—and returns `{ acknowledged: true, deletedCount: 1 }`. (Key Takeaway: `deleteOne()` removes at most 1 matching document.)

questions.stem: How do the three deletion tiers in MongoDB rank from narrowest scope (retaining collection & indexes) to widest destruction scope?

options.text: `deleteOne()` / `deleteMany()` (document level) -> `db.<collection>.drop()` (collection + indexes) -> `db.dropDatabase()` (entire database)
`db.dropDatabase()` -> `db.<collection>.drop()` -> `deleteOne()`
`db.<collection>.drop()` -> `deleteMany({})` -> `db.dropDatabase()`

questions.rationale: Document deletion (`deleteOne`/`deleteMany`) removes documents within a collection; collection drop (`db.col.drop()`) removes the collection and its indexes; database drop (`db.dropDatabase()`) removes the entire database and all its collections from disk. (Key Takeaway: MongoDB's 3-tier deletion hierarchy progresses from documents -> collection -> database.)
